title: How do we write negative powers in another form?
description: Five powers with negative exponents are each written as one over a power with a positive exponent. Two of them have a negative base, so the sign needs care. Keeko doubts whether a negative base always gives a negative answer.
teaching_notes: One idea: a negative exponent turns the power over, and the sign of a negative base depends on whether the new exponent is even or odd. Watch for students who give every negative base a negative answer, or who forget the brackets around the base.

source: Write 2 to the power −4, 10 to the power −5, (−7) to the power −2, (−5) to the power −3 and 10 to the power −100 in equivalent forms.
video_script.why: A learner practises writing negative exponents as fractions, and sees how the sign of a negative base is decided by the exponent.
video_script.substitution: the book's own five powers with negative exponents
video_script.anchor: five powers with negative exponents written in a column on the board
video_script.wrong_move: keeps a minus sign because the base is negative, ignoring the even exponent
video_script.payoff_line: Each negative exponent turns the power over into one over the power

final_answer.spoken: one over sixteen, one over one lakh, one over forty nine, negative one over one hundred and twenty five, and one over ten to the power one hundred

video_script.fraction_reading: 1/16 is read one over sixteen, and −1/125 is read negative one over one hundred and twenty five
video_script.design: One idea: turn the power over, then decide the sign from the new exponent. Wrong idea: a negative base always gives a negative answer. Each power crosses the bar one at a time, and the brackets stay around the negative bases; the last sign only appears at the answer.

beats.on_screen: title card From your book; the five powers 2^-4, 10^-5, (−7)^-2, (−5)^-3, 10^-100 in a column with a question mark

marks.first: 2^-4 and 10^-5 are written in the column
marks.ask: a question mark glows beside the column

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This question is from your book.
<bookmark mark='first'/>We have two to the power negative four, and ten to the power negative five.
<bookmark mark='next'/>Next comes negative seven in brackets, to the power negative two.
<bookmark mark='after'/>After that, negative five in brackets, to the power negative three.
<bookmark mark='last'/>The last one is ten to the power negative one hundred.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How do we write each of them in an equivalent form?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: 3^-2 above a fraction bar crosses the bar and becomes 1/3^2; the exponent loses its minus sign

marks.above: 3^-2 is written above a fraction bar
marks.cross: 3^-2 slides across the bar and becomes 1/3^2
marks.sign: the minus sign of the exponent fades as the power crosses

narration: <bookmark mark='above'/>Take three to the power negative two, sitting above a bar.
<bookmark mark='cross'/>When it crosses the bar, it becomes one over three squared.
<bookmark mark='sign'/>The exponent loses its minus sign when the power crosses.

marks.given: the five powers are written in a column

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, five powers, and each one has a negative exponent.

beats.on_screen: To find: each power as one over a power with a positive exponent

marks.find: the words each power as one over a power with a positive exponent are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to write each power as one over a power with a positive exponent.
<bookmark mark='turn'/>Step one, take two to the power negative four. It turns over to one over two to the power four, which is one over sixteen.
<bookmark mark='ten'/>Then take ten to the power negative five. It turns over to one over ten to the power five.
<bookmark mark='val'/>Ten to the power five is one lakh, so this is one over one lakh.

marks.turn: (−7)^-2 is turned over into 1/(−7)^2, the brackets stay

narration: <bookmark mark='turn'/>Step two, take negative seven in brackets, to the power negative two. It turns over to one over the bracket squared.
<bookmark mark='val'/>Negative seven times negative seven is positive forty nine, so this is one over forty nine.

marks.turn: (−5)^-3 is turned over into 1/(−5)^3, the brackets stay

narration: <bookmark mark='turn'/>Step three, take negative five in brackets, to the power negative three. It turns over to one over the bracket cubed.
<bookmark mark='val'/>Three negative fives multiplied give negative one hundred and twenty five, below the bar.

marks.long: 10^100 is left as a power because it is too long to write out

narration: <bookmark mark='turn'/>Step four, take ten to the power negative one hundred. It turns over to one over ten to the power one hundred.
<bookmark mark='long'/>That number is too long to write out, so we leave it as a power.

marks.pay: the five turned over powers are boxed
marks.ans: 1/16, 1/100000 and 1/49 are written in a column
marks.last: −1/125 and 1/10^100 are added to the column

narration: <bookmark mark='pay'/>Each negative exponent turns the power over into one over the power.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The forms are one over sixteen, one over one lakh, and one over forty nine.
<bookmark mark='last'/>Then negative one over one hundred and twenty five, and one over ten to the power one hundred.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble: (−7)^-2 = −1/49, struck out; (−7)^2 = 49 beside it
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks negative seven to the power negative two is negative one over forty nine. The base is negative, so Keeko keeps the minus sign.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the new exponent is two, and two negatives multiplied give a positive.
<bookmark mark='all'/>Only an odd exponent keeps the minus sign, as with negative five cubed.
